title: Deer Hunter color grading part of story telling?

commenti.body: Color grading is relatively new, so unless you’re watching a remastered version, I don’t believe the version you’re seeing is color graded. I may be wrong though. You’re seeing good staging, location scouting and lighting.

Maybe color grading was too specific or too modern of a term. I guess I mean whatever process (type of film, exposure, development?) was used that provided the vivid colors in some scenes and the much darker colors in other scenes.

For example; I had heard the Matrix used a green tint for all scenes within the Matrix while the real world scenes did not.

It's just that the colors popped so vividly in some scenes in the Deer Hunter, I was curious if there might be some kind of story telling intentionality.
I mean aren’t you basically right? They probably just picked different film stock for different locations/scenes, right?

You had what's called color timing, where usually cinematographers would tell the labs, "Go a few degrees more blue with this stock I'm sending." Some cinematographers would do the color timing themselves when developing, so after the days shoot they'd go to the processing lab and oversee it.
Color timing was what was used before color correction. Some directors like Paul Thomas Anderson still use it.

> They probably just picked different film stock for different locations/scenes, right?

No, they wouldn't have. There weren't really any other options for colour motion picture film than Eastman Kodak in the seventies, and Eastman didn't even offer stocks with different speeds before the eighties. So practically the whole industry had only one colour film stock available at a time.

In any case, I didn’t mean to derail your thread. Apologies. My answer to your question, in my personal opinion, is no. At least when watching that movie, color wasn’t a pronounced aspect. I think it’s just well written and well paced; and there’s a litany of literary devices that are used in a subtle fashion that makes it stand out. For example, Christopher Walken’s propensity for gambling having the payoff that it does was something I didn’t see coming.

That's really interesting to consider. So if a director had wanted to fine tune the colors as part of a narrative tool, they would have to clearly communicate that to whoever was doing the developing of the film. Perhaps something like; "For these scenes, develop longer so we get more saturation." Or, "For this scene develop shorter to mute the colors" or something like that. I don't know what the exact relationship between timing and colors is, but wasn't something that could just be more quickly swapped around like nowadays.

To clarify, colour timing is not done during the development of the negative. It's done during the printing of the dailies or the answer print by manipulating the colour of the light source in the contact printing machine, so it's not something baked into the original negative.

I think the word you're looking for is color timing or unusual film lab processing.

I think when most people use the word color grading, they're referring to the use of computers to alter the color. 

Ironically a period film, Oh brother where out there" was the first Hollywood feature to completely use digital grading.

Now what I think happens occasionally, is that some film remasters get botched colors for that particular edition of that movie.

Batman Returns getting a soft blue for a shadowy scenes instead of black comes to mind. (The 2019 high definition version comes to mind)

The color grading in "Deer Hunter" seems to be a deliberate choice by the filmmakers to enhance the storytelling. The intense colors in the hunting scenes, such as vibrant greens, blue skies, and white snow-capped peaks, likely aim to depict the beauty and serenity of nature. On the other hand, the darker and night scenes in Vietnam create a contrasting and somber atmosphere. It's possible that different filming techniques and equipment were used in various locations, but the distinctive color grading appears to serve a purpose in conveying the mood and setting of the different scenes.
